title: Timeouts and circuit breakers
summary: Limit waiting with timeouts and pause calls to a failing service with a circuit breaker. Trace closed, open, and half-open states using a small model.
introduction: If the library's label printer stops responding, the desk should not wait forever. It can stop waiting and pause new print attempts for a while. Timeouts and circuit breakers give software similar limits.
learningObjectives: Explain a timeout and an overall deadline
Trace closed, open, and half-open breaker states
Choose an honest fallback when a dependency is unavailable

blocks.text: A **timeout** limits how long one operation waits. An **overall deadline** limits the whole job, including waits and retries. If a page has a two-second budget, three separate two-second waits will not fit it.
A **circuit breaker** watches suitable failures from another service. In the **closed** state, calls are allowed. After enough failures, it becomes **open** and rejects new calls quickly for a while.

After a cooldown, the breaker becomes **half-open** and allows a limited test call. If recovery looks good under the chosen rule, it closes. If the test fails, it opens again. These names describe a switch, not whether a request is public or private.

items: This model opens the breaker after two failures in a row.
Two failed calls change the state from closed to open. A new call is blocked.
A cooldown event moves it to half-open. One probe call is allowed.
A successful probe closes this simple breaker. Real policies may need several successful probes before normal traffic returns.

blocks.text: This small JavaScript model runs in the playground. Its numbers and events are chosen for learning. It does not create servers or measure a real service.

blocks.title: Timeouts and circuit breakers model

blocks.text: The third call is blocked even though its sample result is true. The open breaker does not contact the dependency. After the modeled cooldown, the probe gets a chance.

A real breaker needs clocks, a limited number of probes, and a policy for which failures count. Many designs use a rolling error-rate window rather than consecutive failures. The small model teaches states only.

rows: Can reject a slow request that would have succeeded
Avoids repeatedly calling a dependency likely to fail
Needs safe cooldown and recovery rules
Can keep a limited part of the app useful
Must be honest, such as showing an older cover rather than claiming a checkout succeeded

blocks.text: Stopping the caller's wait does not prove the remote job stopped. Cancel work where supported, but still use safe rules if a write might have completed.
A timeout that is too long ties up resources; one that is too short creates needless errors and retries. Use measurements such as slow-end response times, then set a budget that fits the user's task.

items: Change the final probe result from true to false. What is the final state?
It is open. A failed half-open probe tells this model to pause calls again.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not use a fallback that invents success for an important write. If a checkout could not be confirmed, say so and provide a safe next step.
